newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO in security cooperation after Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO in security cooperation after Hebron.

text.p: Four months after Israeli-PLO gunbattles erupted across the West Bank and Gaza Strip, joint Palestinian and Israeli units are patrolling the streets of Hebron to keep Middle East peace moves on track.

"You are a nucleus of peace," Israeli Colonel Munir Dahir told Palestinian and Israeli troops on Wednesday at a windswept hilltop base shared by the sides southeast of Hebron, the West Bank town Israel handed over to the PLO last week after months of acrimonious talks.

"Your job is to go out together as one company on a joint patrol," Dahir told the two four-man teams, who wore nearly identical olive drab uniforms distinguished only by the Israeli and Palestinian insignia gracing their berets and belt buckles.
"It is important that the everyday citizen see you on the hill together, see that there is cooperation and perfect coordination."

The Israeli troop pullback from 80 percent of Hebron, a city of 100,000 Palestinians and 400 Jewish settlers, revived Israeli-PLO peace deals that were nearly doomed in the fierce clashes last September. Sixty Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed in that fighting.
Security coordination between Israel and the PLO -- a centrepiece of their interim peace deals -- has been slowly restored since the unprecedented battles.
The military men responsible for joint security in Hebron, a tinderbox of Jewish and Arab militancy, see tight coordination between them as key to keeping a lid on the volatile city.
"There is an agreement. We are implementing it exactly... and we don't face any problems," Palestinian Colonel Hassan Hijazi told reporters.

"We in Hebron have complete trust with the Israeli officers. There is continuing cooperation between us and them," Hijazi said before dispatching PLO patrol 72 to tour hilltops above a Jewish enclave in Hebron's heart with its Israeli counterpart.

Two orange-flagged jeeps snaked their way down the rocky hilltop lined with olive groves and squat stone houses towards Hebron. Upon entering the PLO-ruled enclave, the Palestinian jeep took the lead.
"When I am with them there, I feel secure," Shai, an Israeli soldier who takes part in the joint patrols in self-ruled Hebron, said of his Palestinian escorts.

Under the Hebron deal, four joint Israeli-Palestinian units patrol self-ruled parts of Hebron and surrounding areas. Joint units are allowed into Israeli-run parts of the city only to deal with security cases not involving Jews there.
Some 20,000 Palestinians remain in the Israeli-controlled sector of Hebron around the tomb of the patriarch Abraham, a shrine sacred to Moslems and Jews.

While many Palestinians grumble that the deal has left one- fifth of Hebron under occupation, PLO police see upholding the interim peace deal as a key to building the trust needed to ensure future Israeli withdrawals in the West Bank.
"We hope this cooperation will lead to success in the peace process and, if God wills, completion of redeployments in other areas," Palestinian First Lieutenant Amer Abdallah said.
